extracted.intended_audience: readers and subscribers of science fiction magazines; short-fiction readers and writers
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative review of two professional science-fiction magazines (Analog and Asimov's), evaluating the magazines and individual stories on literary/technical grounds and advising potential subscribers and writers. The page mixes close readings of stories with broader commentary about editorial stance and market effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary vs technical emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Asimov's regularly presents more "literary" stories, with arguably better writing and definitely a greater emphasis on psychology, imagery and mood than Analog's "nuts-and-bolts" approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to judge a magazine's editorial orientation: does it prioritize character, imagery and mood (Asimov's) or hard extrapolation, technical detail and ideas-driven plots (Analog)? Example/anti-pattern: Asimov's stories that read like slice-of-life are typical of the 'literary' side; Analog favors extrapolation and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential speculative dependence (could only be SF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story is "science fiction in the sense it could not take place in the modern world" (i.e., its speculative elements are essential to the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stories where the speculative premise is central rather than merely background. Examples: Aldiss' 'Safe!' is claimed to be SF in this sense; many literary pieces could be transposed to the present and thus feel less fundamentally SF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting-dependence vs transplantable theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that "could as easily have been set in any present-day country" (criticised as too typical of literary SF) versus stories whose themes depend on the speculative setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether speculative trappings are necessary to the theme or merely decorative. Anti-pattern: dystopias that merely retell present-day refugee situations without leveraging speculative possibilities (example: critique of 'Yellow Card Man').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose quality and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of writing: 'well-written', 'literary flair', or conversely 'terrible writer', 'clunky prose'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sentence-level craft, voice, clarity and elegance. Specific subcriteria mentioned: fluency, avoidance of digression, and whether prose supports or undermines storytelling. Example issues: Sawyer's 'clunky' prose vs Swanwick's confident literary hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and emotional depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories judged by their ability to portray emotional conflicts and human relationships (e.g., 'a powerful story of a mother's love... guilt and forgiveness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for believable motivations, internal conflict, and showing rather than telling ('ability to show rather than to tell'). Strong characterization can redeem weaker prose; poor showing is a common complaint (Sawyer: knows human nature but often fails to show it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story feels fresh or 'too typical' of a substyle (e.g., 'too typical of "literary" SF').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge on whether the story brings new angles, premises or insights rather than rehashing familiar tropes. Anti-pattern: competent but derivative pieces that leave no new impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorability / lasting impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a story sticks with the reader ('forgettable', 'I won't remember a thing about it a month from now').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a retrospective quality metric: emotional resonance, distinctive images, or plot hooks increase memorability; disposable entertainments often score low here (examples: 'Double Dead', 'Diatomaceous Earth').

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement, pacing and curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story makes the reader 'want to find out what happened next' and functions as a 'page-turner'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plot momentum, scene construction and hook effectiveness. Even with weak prose, strong pacing and plot can keep a reader invested (example: Sawyer's serialized plot keeps the reviewer looking forward to the next installment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of twist endings and narrative cheats
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoidance of cheap 'cheat' endings (e.g., revelation that 'nothing that happened before was true' or 'and then he woke up').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalize resolutions that feel like contrived reversals rather than earned developments. Example: Swanwick's novella criticized for ending as an illusion; anti-pattern is the wake-up/twist that invalidates reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific and factual depth in non-fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and level of technical detail in magazine non-fiction: 'contains graphs and scientific notation; not written for scientists, it nevertheless presumes its readers are not liberal arts majors'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether science articles match the audience's literacy (use of graphs, math) and add value. For Analog, scientific rigor and technical exposition are a feature; for readers expecting purely popular summaries, this may be a mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial voice and intellectual prompting
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials that 'ask his readers to think' rather than offer prescriptive solutions (example: Stanley Schmidt's editorial questioning the purposes of public education).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the editorial for whether it provokes thought, frames debates, and matches the magazine's mission. Editorial tone can set expectations for the magazine's intellectual level and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical extrapolation and relevance to current trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that engage with and extrapolate contemporary movements or debates (example: open-source model applied to a moon race; X-Prize analogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value stories that take real-world trends and extrapolate plausible near-future consequences. Such engagement can make SF feel topical and meaningful (example praised: 'Openshot').

rubrics_metrics.name: Series / serialization and recurring-character usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of series/serial installments ('one of a series', 'third instalment of Rollback') and recurring characters as a magazine practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a serialized installment works on its own or depends on prior pieces; weigh reader investment in returning series versus desire for standalone completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre mix (fantasy, slice-of-life, hard SF) and reader fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of fantasy and slice-of-life stories among SF offerings, and whether such pieces align with the reader's tastes ('If fantasy and slice-of-life fiction are not your cup of tea; if you prefer extrapolation plain philosophy instead, you would be better off having a look at Analog').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match magazine content to reader preference: some readers seek mood/psychology (Asimov's), others seek extrapolation/political ideas (Analog). Diversity is a feature for some, a liability for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political / ideological bent
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines may have a discernible political tradition (e.g., 'a long-standing libertarian tradition in... Analog').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that ideological slant can shape story selection and themes; readers' enjoyment may correlate with alignment to that slant. Use as a criterion when recommending magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and interest of ancillary content (poetry, columns, reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-fiction and ancillary items (poems, book columns) can be 'entirely forgettable' or of interest depending on reader priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the mix and quality of columns, reviews and poetry as part of the issue's value. Some readers skip poetry or columns; others value the broader field context they provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor and satire effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether satirical or comic pieces land ('written with the practiced hand of an old master, is engaging and sometimes funny, but still feels like something the writer tossed off').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauge whether humor is fully realized and contributes thematically; half-hearted satire may entertain briefly but not endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling (dramatic technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's tendency to 'show' rather than 'tell' human nature and emotion ('Sawyer's understanding of human nature is strong; his ability to show it, rather than to tell you about it, is almost non-existent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize scenes that dramatize inner life and relations over expository summary. Failure to show weakens characterization even when the underlying insight is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writerly-commercial advice: authenticity over pandering
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need to 'pander to the geo-prejudices of the Yanks' if you tell a story people want to read (note about Sawyer setting books in Canada yet being published in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authors: focus on telling compelling stories rather than altering setting/voice purely for perceived market tastes. Authenticity can succeed across markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation and economic support metric (subscribe to support short fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical recommendation: subscribe to one or both magazines to support the long-term survival of popular short fiction ('if even 10 of you do it, you'll make a difference').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subscribing as both a personal enjoyment decision and a vote for the medium's viability; economic participation is presented as an evaluative criterion for readers deciding whether to support a publication.
